title: Remoteness limits recovery to damage sufficiently connected with the tort

content.overview: Remoteness limits recovery to damage sufficiently connected with the tort. Modern law asks whether the kind of damage was reasonably foreseeable; an intervening event may break causation in appropriate circumstances.
content.glance: Remoteness limits recovery to damage sufficiently connected with the tort. Modern law asks whether the kind of damage was reasonably foreseeable; an intervening event may break causation in appropriate circumstances.
content.study: Remoteness limits recovery to damage sufficiently connected with the tort. Modern law asks whether the kind of damage was reasonably foreseeable; an intervening event may break causation in appropriate circumstances.\n\nRe Polemis used a direct-consequence approach; The Wagon Mound shifted the common-law test toward reasonable foreseeability. Hughes v Lord Advocate shows that the precise manner of occurrence need not be foreseeable if the kind of damage was foreseeable.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Re Polemis used a direct-consequence approach; The Wagon Mound shifted the common-law test toward reasonable foreseeability. Hughes v Lord Advocate shows that the precise manner of occurrence need not be foreseeable if the kind of damage was foreseeable.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: Remoteness is distinct from factual causation. The court first asks whether the breach was a factual cause and then whether legal responsibility extends to the consequence. Thin-skull principles may affect extent of injury.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Factual causation. 2. Identify the kind of damage. 3. Apply reasonable foreseeability. 4. Consider intervening acts. 5. Apply thin-skull and mitigation principles where relevant.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Medical, scientific and expert evidence may establish causal chains. The claimant proves causation overall; remoteness and intervening acts are analysed on the facts.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: Plead the causal chain and heads of loss. Anticipate novus actus arguments. Limitation depends on the underlying tort and statute.

distinctions.left: Remoteness of Damage & Novus Actus Interveniens
distinctions.right: Factual causation asks whether the harm would have occurred without the breach; remoteness limits legal responsibility.
